title: From the Ark to the Temple — Landing on 10 Tefachim
subtitle: Rav Huna's alternative proof, then applying the measurement to an actual sukkah: does the sechach's own thickness count?
sources: Gemara text: Sefaria (William Davidson Edition). Structure and quiz questions 4-6 cross-checked against the Dafyomi Advancement Forum (dafyomi.co.il) quiz for Sukkah 5. Tosfos: dafyomi.co.il's "Point by Point Summary of Tosfos" (Yaakov Montrose, Kollel Iyun Hadaf). The measurements discussion continues onto 6a.
before: 5a found a working proof for the Ark cover's one-tefach thickness, but noticed it only cleanly fits one view of how the table's border was built. This amud opens with Rav Huna's completely independent proof — sidestepping that whole problem via a wordplay on "face" (panim).

Then the amud turns from "how tall was the Ark" to "does that actually tell us anything about a sukkah" — and the answer takes real work: the Gemara has to prove the 10 tefachim is measured to the sukkah's floor, not including the thickness of the sechach itself, by reaching all the way to the dimensions of the Temple.

flow.label: Rav Huna's proof: "upon the face of the cover" — no face is under a tefach
Tested against a giant bird's face and a tiny bird's face — both rejected
flow.sub: settled instead as a wordplay between "face" here and "face" elsewhere in the Torah, refined to mean the cherubs' faces specifically

flow.label: New question: does sukkah's 10-tefachim minimum include the sechach's own thickness, like the Ark's did?
No — proven from the Temple's dimensions instead
flow.sub: cherubs stood 1/3 of the building's height; their wingspan, ten tefachim above the ark, is what the Torah itself calls "sechach"

flow.label: But the math only works cleanly for one cubit-size

items.label: Rabbi Meir
items.sub: every cubit = 6 tefachim — the math lands exactly on 10

items.label: Rabbi Yehuda
items.sub: building-cubits = 6, vessel-cubits = 5 — the math lands on 11½ instead

flow.label: For Rabbi Yehuda, the Gemara falls back on a different kind of source entirely
flow.sub: halachah l'Moshe mi'Sinai — an orally transmitted measure, not derived from any verse

flow.label: Objection: aren't all measures actually written in the Torah?
flow.sub: a verse about the seven species is read as a whole catalog of measures — the wheat-measure case begins, continuing onto 6a

flowCaption: One proof settled by wordplay, then a much bigger proof reaching all the way to the Temple's own dimensions.

opinions.claim: The Ark cover's thickness is a tefach, derived from "upon the face (penei) of the Ark cover" — no face is under a tefach.
opinions.basis: Refined via Rav Acha bar Yaakov into a wordplay between "penei" in that verse and "penei" describing the cherubs, rather than a literal human face.

opinions.claim: Every cubit used in the Mishkan and Temple, for buildings and vessels alike, was the same "intermediate" size — 6 tefachim.
opinions.basis: Makes the cherub-height calculation land exactly on 10 tefachim for the sukkah's sechach-height derivation.

opinions.claim: A building-cubit was 6 tefachim, but a vessel-cubit was only 5.
opinions.basis: Same verses, different cubit-size tradition — but this reading makes the same calculation land on 11½ tefachim instead of 10, so the sukkah-measure can't actually be derived this way under his view.

script.speaker: Rav Huna's proof
script.quote: עַל פְּנֵי הַכַּפּוֹרֶת קֵדְמָה, וְאֵין פָּנִים פָּחוֹת מִטֶּפַח.
script.gloss: "Upon the face of the Ark cover, on the east" — and no person's face measures less than a tefach.

script.speaker: Gemara pushes back, twice
script.gloss: Why assume a human face specifically? What about the face of the giant bird bar Yokhani (far bigger), or a sparrow's face (far smaller)? Each time: "grasp for more, you grasp nothing; grasp for less, you have something" — so a plain human face is the right middle measure.

script.speaker: Reframed entirely
script.gloss: Rav Acha bar Yaakov: Rav Huna's derivation isn't really about a literal face at all — it's a verbal analogy between "penei" here and "penei" describing Yitzchak's face elsewhere, ultimately anchored (after more rejected options — God's face, a generic cherub's face) to the specific size of the cherubs' own faces, a tefach, known by tradition.

script.speaker: New question: does this even apply to sukkah cleanly?
script.gloss: How do we know a sukkah's 10-tefachim minimum excludes the sechach's own thickness? Maybe, like the Ark (measured base-to-top-of-cover), the sukkah's 10 tefachim should include the roofing.

script.speaker: Answered from the Temple
script.quote: אֶלָּא מִבֵּית עוֹלָמִים גָּמַר... כְּרוּבִים בִּשְׁלִישׁ הַבַּיִת הֵן עוֹמְדִין.
script.gloss: The sukkah measure isn't from the Ark after all — it's from the eternal Temple. The cherubs there stood 10 cubits tall, exactly a third of the Temple's 30-cubit height. Applying the same one-third ratio to the (10-cubit-tall) Mishkan works out the cherubs' own height there, and from there, the height of their outstretched wings above the Ark — which the Torah itself calls "sechach." That's the source that sechach sits at least 10 tefachim up, separate from the space below.

script.speaker: One more check
script.gloss: How do we know the wings were spread above the cherubs' heads, and not level with them (which would eat into the 10 tefachim)? Because the verse says "upward." And not "extremely" high, either — the verse doesn't repeat the word.

script.speaker: The math has a catch
script.quote: הָנִיחָא לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר... אֶלָּא לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה... מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר?
script.gloss: This calculation works cleanly for Rabbi Meir, who holds all cubits were a uniform 6 tefachim. But Rabbi Yehuda holds building-cubits were 6 tefachim while vessel-cubits were only 5 — on his reckoning the math for the Ark-and-cover's height comes out to 8½ tefachim, leaving 11½ for the cherubs, not a clean 10.

script.speaker: Falls back on oral tradition
script.quote: לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הִלְכְתָא גְּמִירִי לַהּ... שִׁיעוּרִין, חֲצִיצִין, וּמְחִיצִין — הֲלָכָה לְמֹשֶׁה מִסִּינַי.
script.gloss: For Rabbi Yehuda, the 10-tefachim measure isn't derived from these verses at all — it's a halachah transmitted orally to Moshe at Sinai, in the same category as fixed measures, interpositions, and partitions generally.

script.speaker: Gemara objects
script.gloss: But measures aren't purely oral tradition — they're written in the Torah! A verse about the seven species ("a land of wheat, and barley, and vines...") is read entirely as a catalog of legal measures.

script.speaker: First item on that list, cliffhanging into 6a
script.gloss: "Wheat" sets the measure for a person entering a tzaraat-afflicted house — continued on 6a.

tosfos.summary: How the two lines of text actually appeared on the tzitz.

points.label: (c) Opinion #2
points.he: אלא יש לפרש זה שלא כנגד זה קדש למ״ד בתחילת שיטה התחתונה ושם בסוף שיטה עליונה
points.en: Not stacked directly on top of each other — rather offset, with "Kodesh Lamed" starting the bottom line and God's name ending the top line.

tosfos.summary: Finishing the case for the tzitz sitting higher on the head rather than the forehead.

points.label: (f) Answer
points.he: היה יכול להניחם במקום שכהן גדול מניח את הציץ
points.en: The ordinary priest could put his tefillin exactly where the High Priest put the tzitz — there's room on the head for both, per Eruvin 95b.

points.label: (h) Answer
points.he: ומתרגמינן בין עינוהי... שהכל בגובה של ראש
points.en: The Aramaic translation renders the relevant phrase "between the eyes" the same way it's used for tefillin — which sit on top of the head, not the forehead.

tosfos.summary: What "if you grasp for more, you grasp nothing" actually means, and why it only works for a genuinely finite choice.

points.label: (a)-(b) Explanation & Question
points.he: יש מפרשים לפי שמדה מרובה אין לה סוף... וכאן אי אפשר לומר כן
points.en: Some explain the principle applies because the larger option is literally unbounded — but that can't be the reason here, since a face has to fit inside the Mishkan either way, so both options are finite.

points.label: (e) Explanation #2
points.he: אם אתה תופש את המועט אין מוציאין אותו מידך שהמועט בכלל המרובה
points.en: The real principle: the smaller amount is always included within the larger one, so it's safe to assume by default — the larger amount needs its own proof before you may claim it.

tosfos.summary: A different read than Rashi on where the Temple's upper story actually was.

points.label: (c) Answer
points.he: היינו משפת הכרובים ולמעלה כדאיתא בפ' המוכר פירות (ב״ב צט:)
points.en: The verse's "twenty cubits" for the inner sanctuary is measured from the top of the cherubs upward — not, as Rashi holds elsewhere, describing a low attic above the Holy of Holies.
